title: Lesson 74: The Security Review: A Full Threat Model for an Agent System
description: How to run a security review and build a full threat model for an agent: start with assets and never-boundaries, map the trust boundaries in the agent's chain, run a defined threat set (prompt injection, tool misuse, excessive agency, data exfiltration), tier by impact, and write down the residual risk a named owner accepts.

questions.question: Per lesson 74, why does a security review for an agent have to start with assets and never-boundaries rather than jumping straight to the attack list?
options: Because the attack list is the same for every agent and needs no local context

Because you cannot decide what to protect against a threat until you have said what that threat is meant to reach, and the asset list in an AI system extends beyond databases to include the integrity of the context the model reasons over and the integrity of the agent's actions
Because threat modeling only cares about confidentiality of stored data
Because naming assets is optional and only matters for auditors after launch
questions.explanation: The lesson follows Microsoft's AI threat-modeling guidance: start by being explicit about what you are protecting. Assets extend beyond databases and credentials to user safety, trust, privacy, the integrity of prompts and contextual data, and the integrity of the agent's actions. The assets exercise also forces the honest question of what action the system should never take, which gives the threat set something concrete to attach to.

questions.question: A support agent can read a customer email, retrieve a policy document, update a CRM row, and call a refund tool. An attacker embeds hostile instructions inside a document the agent will retrieve. Using the lesson's threat model, why does the refund call get stopped even though the model's intent has moved?
options: Because the model's refusal training recognizes the embedded text and refuses to act
Because the retrieved document is validated and rejected before it enters the context window

Because the injection can move the model's intent but cannot override the deterministic boundaries around it: a hard verify step that requires a matching copied receipt, a support-tier identity with no refund permission, and a default-deny policy that logs every call
Because the prompt is hashed against a known-good registry and any new version is dropped
questions.explanation: The worked example shows the injection targets the model, and the defense lives in the wiring around it. The refund tool is gated behind deterministic verify logic that requires a verified matching receipt, the support-tier identity has no refund permission at all, and the gateway applies default-deny so the refund call only succeeds for the human escalation path. What stops the attack is not the model being careful; it is that the action is unachievable from where the agent sits.

questions.question: Per lesson 74, what is the most important requirement for the residual-risk column of a written security review?
options: Every threat must be mitigated so no residual risk remains
Each accepted risk gets a named owner who writes down why it is accepted, because a review that records who accepted each remaining risk is the record a governance board and auditor actually want
Residual risk is only recorded for threats above a token-spend threshold
The column is populated automatically by the vendor's security scanner
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that the residual-risk column is the most important and the one most teams skip. Every accepted risk needs a name and a reason, or it is not a decision, it is an omission. A review that ends with every row mitigated is not being honest, because no agent is fully hardened. Recording who accepted each remaining risk is what makes the review an auditable system that a governance board can sign.
